slides.title: Manufacturing process families
slides.body:
Manufacturing converts raw materials → finished parts. Major families:

**Forming/deforming**: shape WITHOUT removing material.
- **Casting**: pour molten metal into mold. Sand, investment, die-casting. High-volume parts (engine blocks, fittings).
- **Forging**: hammer or press solid metal. Crankshafts, connecting rods, military airframes.
- **Rolling**: between rollers. Sheet, plate, bar, structural shapes.
- **Extrusion**: force through die. Aluminum profiles, plastic pipes.
- **Stamping/forming**: sheet metal into shapes. Car body panels.
- **Deep drawing**: cans, sinks, kitchen pots.
- **Bending, rolling, spinning**: incremental shape changes.

**Machining/subtractive**: remove material.
- **Turning (lathe)**: cylindrical parts. Shafts, screws, bushings.
- **Milling**: rectangular + complex parts. CNC mills are flexible workhorse.
- **Drilling**: holes.
- **Grinding**: high-precision surface finish (Ra < 0.4 μm).
- **EDM (Electrical Discharge Machining)**: erode with sparks. Hard materials, complex shapes.
- **Waterjet**: high-pressure water + abrasive. Any material, no heat.
- **Laser cutting**: thermal cut. Sheet metal, complex 2D shapes.

**Additive (3D printing)**: layer by layer.
- **FDM (Fused Deposition)**: extruded plastic. Cheap, prototyping.
- **SLA (Stereolithography)**: UV-cured resin. High detail.
- **SLS (Selective Laser Sintering)**: laser-fused powder (plastic or metal).
- **DMLS / SLM**: metal powder, fused with high-power laser. Aerospace, medical implants, dental.
- **Binder jetting**: like SLS but binder + later sintering. Higher throughput.
- **WAAM (Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing)**: large metal parts via welding. Aerospace, marine, defense.

**Joining**: combine parts.
- Welding (covered earlier).
- Brazing + soldering: lower-melting filler.
- Adhesive bonding.
- Mechanical (bolts, rivets).

**Finishing**: surface treatment.
- Plating (zinc, chrome, nickel).
- Anodizing (aluminum).
- Powder coating.
- Heat treatment (hardening, tempering).
- Surface texturing (knurling, polishing).

slides.title: CNC machining + the modern factory
slides.body:
**CNC (Computer Numerical Control)**: machines following digital instructions from CAD/CAM.

Workflow:
1. CAD model (SolidWorks, Fusion 360, NX).
2. CAM software generates toolpath (Mastercam, HSMWorks, Fusion 360 CAM).
3. G-code (numerical instructions).
4. CNC machine executes.

**Axes**:
- **3-axis** (X, Y, Z): most common. Limited geometry.
- **4-axis**: add rotary table. Can machine around a part.
- **5-axis**: full 3D + 2 rotations. Aerospace, medical, complex parts. Premium.
- **Mill-turn / multi-axis**: combine milling + turning.

**Cutting speeds + feeds**: critical for productivity + tool life.
- Spindle speed (RPM): function of material, tool, diameter.
- Feed rate (mm/min): material removal.
- Depth of cut.
- Trade-off: faster = shorter tool life. Software (Mastercam Adaptive, Autodesk HSM) optimizes.

**Cutting tools**:
- **HSS (High-Speed Steel)**: general purpose, can be sharpened.
- **Carbide**: most modern cutting. Inserts replaced when dull.
- **Coatings**: TiN, TiCN, AlTiN, diamond. Increase tool life.
- **Ceramic, CBN, diamond**: specialty for hardened steels + non-ferrous.

**Automation + Industry 4.0**:
- **Robotic machine tending**: robot loads/unloads parts. 24/7 operation.
- **Pallet systems**: multiple parts queued.
- **Predictive maintenance**: sensors monitor spindle vibration, current, temperature → predict failures.
- **Digital twins**: virtual replica of machine for simulation + optimization.
- **Machine vision**: in-process inspection, tool wear detection.
- **AI/ML**: optimize cutting parameters, anomaly detection.

**Modern machine shops**:
- Mix of capabilities (mill, turn, EDM, grinder, 3D printer).
- Quality control: CMM (Coordinate Measuring Machine), optical scanners.
- ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) + MES (Manufacturing Execution Systems) coordinate operations.

**Cost structure**:
- Machine: \$50K (manual) - \$2M+ (5-axis CNC).
- Tooling per job: \$50-\$5000.
- Labor: \$30-\$80/hr USA.
- Per-part cost: highly geometry-dependent.

slides.title: Design for Manufacturing (DFM) + additive era
slides.body:
**DFM**: design rules to make parts easier (cheaper, faster, more reliable) to manufacture.

**DFM principles** (by process):

**Machining**:
- Use standard tool sizes (drill bits in standard increments).
- Avoid deep + narrow pockets (tool deflection, breakage).
- Generous fillets in corners (sharper = special tools).
- Through-holes preferred (no flat-bottom drilling).
- Single-axis features when possible (avoid 5-axis if 3-axis can do).
- Tolerance loosely except where critical.
- Standard threads + surface finishes.

**Casting**:
- Uniform wall thickness (avoid hot spots + shrinkage).
- Generous draft angles (1-3°) for mold release.
- Avoid abrupt thickness changes.
- Allow for shrinkage (~1-2% for aluminum, more for steel).

**Stamping/forming**:
- Generous bend radii (≥ material thickness).
- Avoid acute corners.
- Plan for grain direction.
- Allow for spring-back.

**Injection molding** (plastics):
- Uniform wall thickness.
- Generous drafts (0.5-3°).
- Avoid undercuts (need side actions = expensive tooling).
- Plan parting line + gate locations.
- Designed-in ribs + bosses for stiffness without thick walls.

**Additive (3D printing)**:
- Self-supporting overhangs (45°+ from horizontal).
- Hollow with internal support lattices.
- Allow for shrinkage + warping.
- Surface finish typically rougher than machined (post-process if needed).
- Different geometry trade-offs than subtractive.

**DFM benefits**: lower cost, faster production, higher quality, fewer iterations.

**Additive manufacturing's expanding role**:
- **Prototypes**: rapid iteration. Reduced cost vs machining.
- **Tooling**: complex jigs + fixtures + molds. Often quick-turn 3D-printed.
- **Production parts**: increasingly. Aerospace (GE LEAP fuel nozzle, SpaceX rocket parts), medical implants (titanium hip), dental (Invisalign), automotive (BMW), industrial (HP Multi Jet Fusion at scale).
- **Topology-optimized parts**: organic shapes only manufacturable additively. Lightweight aerospace + automotive.

**Hybrid manufacturing**: combine additive (rough shape) + machining (precision surfaces) on same machine. DMG Mori, Mazak.

**Mass customization**: small batches of customized parts economically. AM enables. Used in dental + orthopedic implants, footwear (Adidas 4D printed), aerospace.

**Manufacturing economics shifting**:
- Lower-cost machining + additive enable smaller production runs.
- Mass production still dominant for high-volume (automotive, consumer goods).
- Decoupling location + scale: more distributed manufacturing possible.
- Software-defined manufacturing: parts as code, manufactured on demand.

question.question: Choose manufacturing process
question.goal: Need: 1000 units of a complex aluminum bracket, ~100 g each, weight-critical for aircraft. Multiple internal cavities. Tolerances ±0.05 mm on critical features.

steps.prompt: Annual volume + complexity. Casting vs machining vs additive?

options: Multiple considerations: 1000 is too low for typical aluminum die-casting tooling investment (~\$50-200K). Machining 1000 complex parts is feasible but expensive. Additive (DMLS or SLM) is well-suited: low tooling cost, complex geometries (internal cavities) feasible, weight-optimized topology possible.

steps.reveal: Additive aluminum (DMLS / SLM) likely best fit: low tooling investment, complex internal geometries possible (impossible to machine), weight-optimized topology, aerospace-grade certification possible. Per-part cost ~\$100-500. Total ~\$100K-500K for 1000 units.

options: Higher volume justifies tooling investment. Aluminum die-casting becomes economical: \$200K tooling + \$5/part. Internal cavities require complex cores. Hybrid: cast near-net + machine critical surfaces. ~\$700K total + much faster production.

steps.reveal: 100K volume justifies die-casting tooling. Hybrid (cast + machine critical surfaces) cheaper than 100K additive parts. The crossover from additive to casting depends on volume + geometry. Tooling cost ÷ volume = effective per-part tooling cost; compare to per-part savings.

steps.prompt: Critical insight: manufacturing process choice depends on...

options: Volume × complexity × tolerance × materials × time-to-market × supply chain. Each process has a sweet spot. DFM means designing FOR the chosen process; choosing process for the design is also part of the workflow.

steps.reveal: Multi-dimensional optimization: volume + complexity + tolerance + material + cost. Modern engineers iterate: choose process, design for it; or design feature, find process. Software (Plethora, Fictiv, Xometry quoting) automates real-time cost estimation across processes.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Process choice = volume × complexity × tolerance × cost}}$$ Modern manufacturing offers a spectrum: low-volume (3D printing) → mid-volume (CNC) → high-volume (casting + injection molding). Each process has its sweet spot. DFM means designing FOR the chosen process. Cloud quoting services (Xometry, Fictiv, Plethora) bring real-time visibility to costs across processes. The decoupling of design from manufacturing location is reshaping the industry.

question.question: GE LEAP jet-engine fuel nozzle is famously 3D-printed in metal, replacing a 20-piece assembly. Why?
options: Complex internal geometry (cooling channels) impossible to machine + assemble traditionally. Single 3D-printed part = no joints = no leaks = lighter + more reliable. Cost per part higher than per-piece machining, but lower TOTAL cost (no assembly, no inventory of 20 parts). Aerospace tolerates higher per-part cost for weight + reliability.
question.explanation:
GE LEAP fuel nozzle (2015 launch): single 3D-printed cobalt-chrome part replaces 20-piece welded assembly. Internal cooling channels impossible to machine in single piece. Single part: 25% lighter, 5× more durable, no assembly + leak issues. Per-part cost ~\$3000 (high); total system cost LOWER (no assembly labor, no inventory, no warranty failures). Aerospace tolerates per-part cost for weight + reliability gains. Cumulative LEAP engine deliveries: 30,000+ as of 2024. One of the largest commercial AM success stories.

Generalizes: AM wins where (1) geometry complexity matters, (2) part consolidation saves assembly, (3) weight matters more than cost.

slides.workedSolution: GE LEAP nozzle: 20-part welded assembly → 1 3D-printed part. Internal cooling channels (impossible to machine in one piece). 25% lighter, 5× more durable, no assembly. Per-part cost higher but lower TOTAL cost (no assembly labor, no inventory, fewer failures). Aerospace's high tolerance for per-part cost in exchange for weight + reliability makes AM economical. Now 30K+ in service.

question.question: DFM saves 20% on a part costing \$50. New cost?
Scaling a startup's product
question.prompt: An EV battery-pack startup is going from prototype (1000 units/year) to production (100,000/year). Walk through manufacturing process + supply chain changes needed.
Explain in two or three sentences why additive manufacturing has been called a 'revolution' even though most parts are still made traditionally.
question.rubric: Mentions that AM removes constraints traditional manufacturing imposed (uniform thickness, draft angles, accessible features) + enables geometry optimization + part consolidation; for HIGH-VALUE low-volume applications (aerospace, medical, specialty), AM is genuinely transformative; for MASS-PRODUCED parts, traditional processes remain cheaper at scale. AM's role is growing rapidly + reshaping subsets of manufacturing, not replacing all of it.
